newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean unions threaten total public shutdown.
newsitem.headline: South Korean unions threaten total public shutdown.

text.p: Militant South Korean strike leaders on Wednesday gave the government a one-week deadline to scrap its new labour law or face a total stoppage by public sector workers.
Unless the bill is repealed by midnight on Tuesday, the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions will call for a shutdown of all public services, its leader Kwon Young-kil told a news conference.
The stoppage would begin immediately if state prosecutors carried out their threat to issue arrest warrants against union leaders, Kwon said.

"Subways, telecommunications companies, mints, freight services, newspapers and everyone else not on strike now will start industrial action on January 15 unless the government revokes the law," he said.
"To solve the current pressing problems in a reasonable way, the Korean Confederation is formally proposing a meeting with President Kim Young-sam."

Kim insisted on Tuesday he would not back down and argued that the new law, which makes the labour market more flexible by allowing worker layoffs, was a long overdue move to bring down industrial costs.
Kim also ruled out a meeting with opposition parties to discuss the crisis.
Kwon said the confederation would join forces with all other striking labour groups, including the dominant Federation of Korean Trade Unions, from next Monday.
"Unless these demands are met we have no option but to mobilise all our resources to wage intensive strike struggle," Kwon said.
He accused the president of "trying to crush the whole democratic labour movement".
The confederation, which is outlawed by the government, claims half a million members.

Its union affiliates have a grip on car and ship manufacturing, the main subway lines in Seoul, major media outlets, hospitals, Korea Telecom, the metal industry, construction firms and chemical producers.
In addition it controls the unionised workforce at leading industrial conglomerates, including Hyundai and Daewoo.

The larger Federation of Korean Trade Unions, with 1.2 million workers, is strongest among miners, railway workers, printers, port and postal workers, banking staff and various state industries, including the tobacco monopoly.
There is overlap between the two umbrella union bodies within industries.
In a move to lower the temperature, state prosecutors said they would hold off on a decision to issue arrest warrants until Thursday.
Strikes continued to affect carmakers and shipbuilding yards, although there were conflicting reports about damage to production.
Hyundai Motor said its car plant in Ulsan was working at 60-70 percent capacity with 15,000 out of a total workforce of 32,000 on strike.
Daewoo Motors reported a similar production level. A spokesman for Ssangyong Motors said lines were working normally while the union said they were completely idle.

Some hospital workers and unions at four major broadcaster walked out on Tuesday, but disruption so far has been minimal, with non-union staff at hospitals and television networks keeping services running.
Analysts said damage to the economy so far was relatively minor, and the strikes could even be a short-term blessing in disguise by allowing companies to run down excessive inventories.
"Companies are using the work stoppages to unload inventories," Rhee Namuh, the head of research at Dongbong Peregrine Securities, told Reuters Financial Television.
However, he added the impact of the strikes would be "relatively significant if they drag on".
